summary: This unit teaches you to evaluate an organisation's occupational health and safety (OHS) performance: to plan the evaluation and agree its scope and criteria; to collect evidence from incident data, inspections, audits, surveys and contractors; to calculate and read rates such as the lost-time injury frequency rate; to analyse causes, controls, safety culture and wellbeing; and to report the findings and turn them into an improvement action plan that is carried out and checked.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. **Occupational health and safety (OHS)** is the protection of the health, safety and welfare of people at work. An **OHS performance evaluation** is a planned, evidence-based look at how well an organisation is protecting people, and what it must improve. At Level 5 you plan and lead such evaluations in a ministry, agency, municipal corporation, hospital, school or business, and report to the executive.

An evaluation is not a hunt for someone to blame, and it is not only a response to accidents. It asks: are our arrangements working, how do we know, and what must we do next? The answers come from **data, inspection, audit and the views of the workers themselves**.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: Explain why and what to evaluate
Describe the purpose of evaluation, the employer's general legal duties and the parts of an OHS management system.
Agree scope, criteria, methods, team and timetable before any data are collected.
Use several sources, check data quality, and deal with under-reporting.
Use leading and lagging indicators and calculate frequency rate, severity rate, injury rate and percentages.
Find trends, root causes, weak controls, cultural and wellbeing problems, and the cost of poor performance.
Include contractors, field staff and others whose work the organisation controls or arranges.
Report to the executive, protect confidentiality, prepare an action plan with owners and dates, and check results.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** of scenario questions, including rate and percentage sums.
A **written paper** with short answers (terms such as leading indicator, root cause, audit) and longer answers in full sentences.
**Practical tasks** using made-up OHS data and records: calculate indicators, analyse them and present findings with recommendations.

blocks.note: Learn the formulas in the Indicators section. Work every sum twice, and always state the unit of the answer (per million hours, per 100 workers, days, percentage, J$).
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Why evaluate: duties and the management system

blocks.p: An organisation that only reacts to accidents learns after people have been hurt. Regular evaluation lets the executive **find weaknesses and improve before people are harmed**, check that money spent on safety is working, meet legal duties and show leadership. It is an annual or periodic activity, with checks at other times when something major changes.

Jamaica's occupational safety and health law is described here by purpose, not by section. In general terms, it expects an employer, including a public body, to **provide a safe workplace and manage its risks**. In practice that means:

ul: assess hazards and control the risks;
provide safe equipment, safe systems of work and a safe place to work;
give information, instruction, training and supervision;
consult workers and their safety representatives;
provide welfare facilities and first aid;
prepare for emergencies such as fire and hurricanes;
investigate incidents and report serious injuries and dangerous events to the authorities as required;
look after people who are not employees but are affected by the work, such as contractors and visitors.

blocks.p: An evaluation can use these duties as headings. For each duty it asks whether the arrangements actually work, not just whether a document exists.

blocks.h: The parts of an OHS management system

flow: Planning: hazards, risks, objectives, legal duties
Implementing: controls, training, emergency plans, contractors
Measuring: inspection, incidents, health surveillance, audit

head: Part
What the evaluation looks for
rows: A current OHS policy, signed by the present head of the body and understood by staff. A policy last signed eight years ago by a chief executive who has left needs review and re-signing
Resources, regular review and leaders who follow the rules themselves. A poster in reception, a statement in the annual report or a safety officer with no budget or authority is not enough
Assessments that are current and controls that are in place on site
A working safety committee with staff representatives, which meets and whose actions are completed
Training that changes how work is done, not only attendance records
Plans that are tested, for example by timed drills
Reports are made, causes are found and actions are completed
Inspections, health surveillance and audits happen as planned
Results are reviewed by senior management and used to set the next objectives

blocks.p: A good evaluation is planned before any data are collected. The plan sets out the **scope, criteria, methods and timetable**.

head: Part of the plan
Questions to answer
rows: Why is it being done, and who will use the results? (for example the chief executive and the board)

Which sites, staff, contractors, activities and periods? An agency with offices in Kingston, Montego Bay and Mandeville should include all sites, staff, contractors and main activities, not only the head office, desk staff or sites that had accidents
The standard used to judge: the law, the organisation's own policy and objectives, targets, good practice for similar bodies
Data analysis, inspection, document review, interviews, surveys, observation, audit
Who does it. Include a member from outside the unit evaluated where possible, for an objective view, plus staff and safety representatives
Dates, travel, access, cost, and when the report is due
How personal and health data will be protected

blocks.p: The **safety committee**, with staff representatives, should take part. Staff know the hazards and can check that the fixes work. Involving them also builds trust, which affects what they report. Consultation does not mean staff approve every management decision.

Some parts should be done by someone from outside the unit being evaluated. An outsider is more objective and sees what insiders have stopped noticing. The unit must still take part, because it holds the knowledge, and the outsider is not there for anyone to blame.

A move to a new building, a new work pattern, new equipment or a new law all bring new risks. An evaluation should cover them. The old building's risks may move with the staff, and the new premises add their own.

blocks.note: Before you start, ask: have we agreed the scope and criteria in writing? An evaluation built to show the findings the executive wants is not an evaluation.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: No single source gives the full picture. Use several, and compare them.

head: Source
What it shows
Watch out for
rows: What happened, where, to whom, the causes and actions
Under-reporting; different forms and categories in different offices
Minor injuries that may never reach incident reports
Not always linked to the accident book
Patterns by unit, reason and season
Must be grouped to protect privacy
Conditions at a point in time
Only a snapshot; depends on who inspects
Whether the whole system meets its criteria and works
Early signs of harm, such as hearing loss
Culture, stress, willingness to report, how work is really done
Anonymous surveys give more honest answers
Safety performance of those working for the body
Records show activity, not always effect

blocks.p: A **workplace inspection** looks at physical conditions and behaviour at a place and time. An **audit** is a systematic and independent check of whether the whole OHS management system meets its stated criteria and works in practice. An inspection is not done only by outside experts, and an audit does not check only first-aid boxes.

Before analysing two years of incident reports from several offices, check that the data are **complete and recorded the same way**: the same definitions of an injury, a lost-time injury and a near miss, the same forms and the same period. If each office used its own categories, the figures cannot be compared.

**Under-reporting** is the failure to report injuries and incidents, which makes figures look better than they are. Signs: a sharp fall in reported injuries while first-aid supplies, absence and complaints stay the same or rise; staff who say "nothing ever happens" when they report a hazard; targets or bonuses linked to low injury numbers.

ul: Compare incident reports with first-aid records, absence and survey answers.
Recommend a **no-blame reporting system**, simple forms, feedback to reporters and removal of rewards for low numbers.
Treat a sudden fall in reports as a question, not as good news.
**Investigations:** a good investigation finds root causes and leads to actions that are done. A weak one names the worker at fault, makes no recommendations and repeats the first report.
**Training:** if 95% completed manual handling training but back injuries have not fallen, check whether the training changed how the work is done.
**Emergency arrangements:** timed drills showing that everyone left safely are better evidence than a written plan in a file.
**Controls:** check that controls such as handrails are in place and that incidents they were meant to prevent have fallen.

blocks.p: A public body that uses contractors still has duties for work done on its behalf. The evaluation should look at how contractors are chosen (safety records asked for and scored), the contract terms, induction and supervision on site, incident reporting and the right to stop unsafe work.

Health surveillance results, such as hearing tests, must appear in the report **grouped so that no individual can be identified**. Do not post names or results on a noticeboard, send them to all managers or print them in the report.

Workplace health includes stress, workload, bullying and abuse from the public. These are **psychosocial hazards**: hazards from work design, workload, harassment and stress rather than physical things. They are workplace hazards that need risk controls, not private matters for each worker to handle alone, and they belong in an OHS evaluation. Useful evidence includes grouped absence data, turnover, grievances, use of the employee assistance programme, exit interview themes and an anonymous wellbeing survey.

head: Type
What it measures
Examples
Strength and weakness
rows: Lost-time injuries, injury frequency rate, days lost, compensation costs
Shows real outcomes and allows comparison, but comes too late to prevent harm, can be distorted by under-reporting, and small numbers can move by chance
Percentage of planned inspections completed, percentage of hazard reports closed on time, percentage of staff trained, audit scores, drills completed
Shows prevention while there is time to act, but must be linked to real effect

blocks.p: A balanced set uses both. A poor measure is one that counts effort without effect, such as the number of safety posters printed.

A useful target is specific, measurable and has a date and an owner: "close 90% of hazard reports within 30 days this year". "Make safety a little better" or "zero accidents whatever it takes" are not good targets.

head: Measure
Formula
Unit
rows: Number of lost-time injuries x 1,000,000 / hours worked
Days lost per million hours worked
Number of injuries / number of workers x 100
Days lost / number of lost-time injuries

blocks.note: The base of one million hours is the one used in this unit. Some bodies use 200,000 hours. Always say which base you use and use the same one when you compare. Follow the base your instructor or organisation sets.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Question
Working
Answer
rows: A body recorded 6 lost-time injuries in 1,200,000 hours. LTIFR?
The same body lost 240 days. Severity rate?
18 injuries among 600 workers. Rate per 100 workers?
8 lost-time injuries cost 96 working days. Days per injury?
Agency A: 10 injuries, 500 staff. Agency B: 15 injuries, 1,000 staff. Which rate is higher?
A has the higher rate per 100 staff, although B had more injuries

blocks.note: Compare rates, not raw numbers. Agency B had more injuries, but it also has twice as many staff. Always convert to a rate before you compare units or years of different size.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Year 1: 8 lost-time injuries, 2,000,000 hours, 160 days lost. Year 2: 5 lost-time injuries, 1,250,000 hours, 175 days lost.

The frequency rate did not change, but injuries became more serious (35 days against 20), and the severity rate rose from 80 to 140. A report that said "fewer injuries" without the rates would mislead.

Compare your rates with similar organisations as well as with your own past results. This shows whether performance is good for the sector, and not only whether it has improved. Use the same definitions when you compare.

Direct costs (treatment, compensation, repairs) are only part of the cost. **Indirect costs** include overtime to cover absent staff, lost output, investigation time, damaged equipment, training replacements and lowered morale. Total cost = direct + indirect. If direct costs were J$2,400,000 and indirect costs J$7,200,000, the total is **J$9,600,000**. Showing the total cost helps the executive see safety as an investment.

ul: Compare several years, not one. Use rates, so changes in staff and hours are allowed for.

Break the data down by site, unit, job, type of injury, time and cause. For example, slips and falls that rise from 12 to 20 over three years, mostly in one ward, point the evaluation to that ward to find the causes and controls.
Beware of small numbers: a rise from 2 to 3 may be chance. Look at near misses and leading indicators as well.

blocks.p: A **root cause** is the deepest underlying reason an incident happened, often found by asking "why?" several times. "Driver error" is not a root cause. If three forklift incidents in a warehouse are each blamed on driver error, the evaluation should look at **training, supervision, layout and work pressure**. Stopping at blame means the same incident will happen again.

flow: Action that removes the root cause

blocks.h: Judge the controls: the hierarchy of control

head: Level
Control
Example (noisy machine)
rows: Job rotation, shorter exposure, signs, training

blocks.p: The **hierarchy of control** ranks ways of controlling a hazard, from elimination at the top down to PPE. PPE is the **last line of defence**. If most controls for a depot's noisy machines rely on ear protection, the evaluation should recommend looking for quieter machines or enclosures first, not removing ear protection or asking staff to put up with the noise.

ul: Look at the outcome. After handrails were fitted, falls on the stairs dropped from 9 to 2 a year: record this as **evidence that the control is working**. Falls did not reach zero, but that does not make it a failure, and it is no reason to remove the handrails.
Look at the quality of use. Rules that are not followed, guards that are removed and equipment that is not maintained are signs that the control design or supervision has failed.

blocks.p: **Safety culture** is the shared attitudes and habits that shape how people act on safety when no one is watching. Injury figures alone cannot measure it. Use an anonymous survey, interviews and focus groups, observation of practice and a review of how managers respond to reports. When staff say they do not report hazards because "nothing ever happens", it shows that **trust in management's response is low**, not that staff do not care or that there are no hazards.

If sickness absence in a unit is double the average and staff mention long hours, look into workload and stress as possible causes. Do not assume that the unit is lazy, and do not drop its figures. High stress and verbal abuse in a call centre are hazards that need controls such as call-handling procedures for abusive callers, rest breaks, supervisor support and counselling.

When office staff report neck and wrist pain, useful evidence is **workstation assessments and records of complaints**, not building details or opening hours of a pharmacy. Where hearing tests or similar results are used, report them in groups only.
At the start of this year's evaluation, check which of last year's recommendations were done and whether they worked. Repeating them without checking, or ignoring them, breaks the improvement cycle.

The executive needs a short report that helps them decide. It should contain **trends, key risks, progress on actions and decisions needed**. It should not copy every incident form in full, with names, or list every injured worker, and it should not show only good news.

head: Part
Contents
rows: Main findings and the decisions asked of the executive, on one page
What was evaluated, against what criteria, using what evidence
Key leading and lagging indicators, with two or three years of trends and, where possible, a benchmark; a simple chart or dashboard
Main problems, root causes, controls that work and controls that do not
Cost of incidents in J$, legal and reputation risks, the risk of doing nothing
Prioritised, each with a proposed owner, date and cost
Done, partly done, not done, and effect

blocks.p: If you have 10 minutes with the board, **lead with the key trends, risks and decisions needed**. Do not read every figure from a 50-page report.

If an evaluation finds that a serious injury was not reported to the authorities as the law requires, recommend that it is **reported now and the reporting procedure is fixed**. Never delete the record or wait for someone to ask.

blocks.h: From findings to an action plan

flow: Rank findings by risk and legal duty
Write an action that deals with the root cause
Prefer controls high in the hierarchy
Give each action an owner, date, cost and measure
Executive approves and resources the plan
Feed lessons into the next evaluation

ul: Rank twelve recommendations by risk and give each an owner and a date. Do not hand all of them to the safety officer alone, do the cheapest first whatever the risk, or wait for next year.
The action plan is monitored regularly, for example monthly, by the safety committee, and reported to the executive each quarter.
The improvement cycle is complete only when actions are **carried out and their effect checked**. Filing the report is not the end.

blocks.p: Set targets that are measurable. For example: lost-time injury frequency rate below 4.0; 90% of hazard reports closed within 30 days; 95% of planned inspections completed; every site drill timed and recorded.

blocks.note: An evaluation that only describes problems helps no one. An action plan with owners, dates and checks changes the workplace.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: explain why an organisation evaluates its OHS performance and what the law generally expects of an employer.
describe the parts of an OHS management system and what an evaluation looks for in each.

use several sources of evidence and check that data are complete and consistent.
recognise and deal with under-reporting.

calculate LTIFR, severity rate, injury rate per 100 workers, days lost per injury and percentages, and compare rates not raw numbers.

A measure of harm that has already happened, such as lost-time injuries.
Lost-time injury frequency rate: lost-time injuries x 1,000,000 / hours worked.
Failure to report injuries and incidents, which makes figures look better than they are.
A systematic and independent check of whether an OHS management system meets its criteria.
A look at conditions and behaviour at a workplace at a point in time.
The joint group of management and staff representatives that discusses health and safety.

Personal protective equipment, the last line of defence against a hazard.

Comparing your performance with that of similar organisations.

c1.title: A municipal works depot
c1.text: A municipal corporation in St Catherine has a works depot with 150 workers. This year they worked 300,000 hours and had 6 lost-time injuries, with 90 working days lost. Last year the depot had 4 lost-time injuries in 320,000 hours. The depot manager, Mr Winston Lee, says six injuries is "a small number" and nothing to worry about.

c2.title: Field officers and vehicles
c2.text: A ministry's field officers drive to farms and communities across the island. Over two years there were 11 vehicle incidents, and each report says "driver error". The ministry planned 36 vehicle inspections last year and completed 27. Officers say they are given too many visits to complete in a day.

c3.title: A public body's call centre
c3.text: A public body's call centre in Kingston has 80 staff. Sickness absence is 8%, compared with 4% in the rest of the body. An anonymous staff survey shows high stress and frequent verbal abuse from callers. Staff say supervisors are always too busy to help and that breaks are often missed.

c4.title: Planning and reporting an evaluation
c4.text: Ms Andrea Campbell, OHS manager of a ministry with offices in four parishes, has been asked to evaluate OHS performance. Reported injuries have fallen by half since managers' bonuses were linked to low injury numbers, but first-aid supply use and sickness absence are unchanged. She must present her findings to the executive in 10 minutes.

c5.title: Costs and contractors in an agency
c5.text: A government agency uses outside firms for security and cleaning. Last year its direct injury costs were J$1,800,000 and indirect costs were estimated at three times that amount. The agency's own audit found that contractors' injuries are not recorded anywhere, and that a serious fall by a cleaner was not discussed by the safety committee.

questions.q: Mr Lee divides the 6 injuries by the 150 workers and multiplies by 100, getting 4.0, and calls it the frequency rate. What is wrong?
o: Nothing is wrong, because frequency is always found per 100 workers each year
He should have divided by the number of days lost, not by the workers
That is the injury rate per 100 workers; the frequency rate uses hours worked
He should multiply by 1,000, not by 100, to get the frequency rate
questions.why: Injuries per 100 workers is a different measure. The lost-time injury frequency rate is 6 x 1,000,000 / 300,000 = 20.0 per million hours worked.

questions.q: The depot's frequency rate this year is 20.0 per million hours. Last year it was 12.5. What does the comparison show?
o: The rate rose by 60%, so performance is worse
The rate rose by 2, so the change is too small to matter
The rate fell, because there were only two more injuries
The rate is the same, because hours worked were similar
questions.why: 20.0 against 12.5 is a rise of 7.5, which is 60% of 12.5. Only a rate, not the raw number of injuries, allows a fair comparison.

questions.q: Mr Lee sets a target to cut the depot's frequency rate of 20.0 by 25% next year. What is the target rate?
Mr Lee says six injuries is a small number. What is the best response from the evaluator?
o: Agree, because six injuries is below the level that the law requires to be reported
Small numbers can mislead, so look at the rate, severity and near misses too
Disagree, because any injury at all means the depot has failed
Agree, but add this year's injuries to last year's total to make the number larger
questions.why: A small number can rise or fall by chance and hide risks. The evaluator reads rates, severity, near misses and leading indicators together.

questions.q: Every vehicle report says "driver error". What should the evaluation look at?
o: Which drivers had the most incidents, so that discipline can be decided
How long each driver has held a licence and the class of licence held
Workload, trip planning, vehicle condition, supervision and training
Whether the driver was injured or only the vehicle was damaged
questions.why: "Driver error" is a description, not a root cause. The evidence that officers have too many visits points to work pressure and planning, which management controls.

questions.q: What percentage of planned vehicle inspections was completed, and what type of indicator is it?
o: 75%; a leading indicator
75%; a lagging indicator
27%; a leading indicator
133%; a lagging indicator
questions.why: 27 / 36 x 100 = 75%. It measures preventive action, so it is a leading indicator.

questions.q: Which recommendation is highest in the hierarchy of control for the vehicle incidents?
o: Send every officer on a defensive driving course this year
Issue bright vests for officers to wear when they leave the vehicle
Put a notice in every vehicle reminding officers to drive carefully
Cut the visits and plan routes so that trips are fewer and shorter
questions.why: Changing the work (fewer, better-planned trips) removes part of the hazard. Training, vests and notices act on people and sit lower in the hierarchy.

questions.q: After the ministry shortens trips, vehicle incidents fall from 11 in two years to 3 in the next year. How should the evaluation treat this?
o: As too small to count, since it covers only one year of figures
As evidence that the control is working, so keep it and monitor it
As a failure, since the number of incidents did not fall to zero
As a result of luck, so the earlier schedule should now return
questions.why: A clear fall after a control is introduced is evidence it works. It is kept and monitored, and one more year of data will strengthen the conclusion.

questions.q: Of the 80 call centre staff, 56 completed the anonymous survey. What percentage is that?
questions.why: 56 / 80 x 100 = 70%. A good response rate matters because the results can then be taken to represent the whole call centre.

questions.q: Which set of evidence would best help the evaluation understand the high absence?
o: Absence by unit and reason, turnover, grievances and focus groups
The call centre's opening hours and the number of calls answered
The cost of the staff canteen and the age of the furniture
The total number of staff working across the whole body
questions.why: Grouped absence and wellbeing data, together with what staff say, point to causes such as workload and abuse. Other items are not linked to the problem.

questions.q: Which action should the evaluation recommend first for abusive callers?
o: Asking staff to stay calm and take more training in customer care
Giving all staff a longer lunch break once a month as a reward
Removing the survey question about abuse so that morale can improve
A procedure that lets staff end abusive calls, with supervisor support
questions.why: A procedure that changes how abusive calls are handled is a control at work-system level. Training and breaks help but leave the hazard in place.

questions.q: The evaluator reports on staff wellbeing from the survey to the executive. How should individual comments be shown?
o: With each worker's name beside their comment for accuracy
Grouped and summarised so that no individual can be identified
On the call centre noticeboard so that staff see it was used
Only to the supervisors who are named in the comments
questions.why: Survey and health information is reported in groups to protect confidentiality, otherwise staff will stop answering honestly.

questions.q: Reported injuries fell by half after bonuses were linked to low injury numbers, but first-aid use and absence did not change. What is the most likely reason?
o: Better safety, because injuries fell and bonuses rose
Staff are using the first-aid supplies for their families
Under-reporting, because staff or managers are avoiding reports
A change in the weather that reduced all accidents
questions.why: When injury reports fall but other indicators do not, under-reporting is likely. Rewards for low figures encourage it.

questions.q: Two offices count any injury with one day off work as lost-time; the other two count only absences of more than three days. What should Ms Campbell do before comparing offices?
o: Agree one definition and recode the data before comparing
Compare the figures as they stand and note the difference
Use only the figures from the offices that count one day
Drop the two offices with the strictest definition
questions.why: Data must be recorded the same way before they are compared. Otherwise differences in definition, not in safety, drive the result.

questions.q: What should Ms Campbell recommend about the managers' injury-number bonuses?
o: Keep the bonuses but make the injury target stricter each year for managers
Keep the bonuses but pay them only to managers of the largest offices
Pay the bonus to staff as well, so that everyone shares the same target
Stop rewarding low injury numbers and reward actions such as hazards closed
questions.why: Rewards for low figures push people to hide injuries. Rewarding preventive action keeps the data honest and encourages the right behaviour.

questions.q: Ms Campbell has 10 minutes with the executive. What is the best approach?
o: Show every injury of the last two years in order of the date
Lead with key trends, risks and decisions needed, on a one-page summary
Describe the history of the ministry's safety committee in detail
Read the full report aloud and leave all questions until later
questions.why: Executives need to decide. A short summary of trends, risks and decisions needed makes the best use of limited time.

questions.q: A guarding programme costs J$1,500,000 and is expected to avoid injuries costing J$600,000 a year in direct costs and J$1,800,000 in indirect costs. About how long will it take to repay its cost?
o: About 18 months
About 2.5 years
About 7.5 months
About 4 months

questions.q: Contractors' injuries are not recorded anywhere. What should the evaluation recommend?
o: Record and review contractors' injuries and put reporting into contracts
Leave contractors' records to the contractors as their own matter
Record contractors' injuries only if they are lost-time injuries
Record the injuries but exclude them from the agency's rates
questions.why: The agency has duties for work done on its behalf. Reporting should be a contract requirement, and the data should be reviewed with its own.

questions.q: Why is it a concern that the safety committee did not discuss the cleaner's serious fall?
o: The cleaner is not entitled to be discussed there
Falls are less important than electrical incidents
The committee should only meet after a death
The system for review and learning is not working
questions.why: A serious incident should be investigated and reviewed with actions agreed. Missing it shows the review and learning part of the system is weak.

questions.q: Which target would best help the agency manage contractors' safety next year?
o: Contractors to have fewer injuries than they had in other earlier years
All contractor injuries reported within 24 hours and reviewed monthly
Contractors to try to report injuries wherever they can do so
The agency to make contractors' safety a little better each year
questions.why: A good target is specific, measurable, dated and owned. The other options are vague or leave the agency with no way to check progress.
